topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: Bridging the AI literacy gap: mixed-methods evidence from employers on workforce readiness and curriculum priorities - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI literacy gap: mixed-methods evidence from employers on workforce readiness and curriculum priorities  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — employer perspectives on AI literacy needs are valuable, but geographic scope, sample size, and sector representation are unclear from the title and snippet alone. Findings may not generalise across all industries or regions equally.
takeaways: Identify specific AI literacy gaps in your workforce by surveying employer priorities on curriculum — use employer feedback to target upskilling programs on high-demand competencies rather than generic AI awareness.

Align your organisation's learning pathways with employer-identified readiness benchmarks — this mixed-methods evidence likely reveals which foundational skills employers prioritise, allowing you to sequence training effectively.
Use these employer-validated curriculum priorities to design or select internal AI literacy programs, ensuring they address workforce readiness gaps rather than theoretical or peripheral AI concepts.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development unclear without seeing full methodology and geographic scope.
takeaways: AI literacy for non-technical learners works best when embedded within a broader digital literacy framework rather than taught in isolation, suggesting workplace AI training should integrate with existing digital competency programmes.

Middle school pedagogical approaches to AI competencies (e.g., conceptual foundations, ethical reasoning, hands-on practice) may inform how to scaffold AI learning for adult employees with varying technical backgrounds.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European public health context; findings on digital competencies may have limited direct application to other sectors or regions, though core competency principles could be adaptable.
takeaways: Identify which digital competencies are most critical for your workforce by reviewing the framework's taxonomy — this helps prioritize upskilling efforts rather than pursuing broad, unfocused digital training.
Use the competency framework to benchmark current capability gaps in your organization and design targeted learning pathways that align with established European standards in digital literacy.
Consider how competencies map across different roles (clinical, administrative, technical) to ensure AI-related training is tailored to job-specific needs rather than one-size-fits-all approaches.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on public health faculty development contexts, likely US-based given the Frontiers journal context, but geographic scope and sample size are unclear from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI literacy is common but can be shifted through structured development programs—design interventions that move staff from skepticism to capability rather than assuming buy-in.

In public health education contexts, positioning AI literacy as a core competency for future practitioners (not an optional add-on) helps frame professional development as career-relevant rather than burdensome.

articles.title: Agents, robots, and us: Skill partnerships in the age of AI - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Agents, robots, and us: Skill partnerships in the age of AI  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey analysis draws on global trends and client work, but specific examples and case studies may skew toward large enterprises in developed economies. Applicability to small-to-medium Australian organisations may vary.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as 'skill partnerships' rather than replacement — focus on identifying which human skills complement AI agents best, and design roles around that complementarity.

Audit your workforce's readiness across three dimensions: technical fluency with AI tools, domain expertise to guide AI outputs, and soft skills for human-AI collaboration — gaps in any of these limit partnership effectiveness.
Start with high-impact, lower-risk use cases to build organisational confidence and skill with AI agents before scaling to mission-critical processes.

articles.title: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey research typically draws on global client work and surveys, but findings may reflect consulting-sector perspectives and clients skewed toward large organisations with training budgets.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation will be most disrupted by gen AI, then prioritise upskilling cohorts in those areas first rather than taking a blanket approach to all staff.
Build learning pathways that combine technical AI literacy with domain expertise—employees need to understand both how gen AI works and how to apply it in their specific function.
Create feedback loops to test reskilling initiatives on small groups before rolling out organisation-wide, as gen AI capability needs evolve rapidly.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology — geographic scope, sample size, and sector representation cannot be determined from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: AI adoption in organisations may have paradoxical effects on creativity: while it can enhance certain creative outputs, it may simultaneously constrain creative thinking or risk-taking in other areas — organisations should assess which creative capabilities matter most and design AI implementation to protect them.

When rolling out AI tools, explicitly address potential psychological or structural barriers that may inhibit creativity (e.g., over-reliance on AI suggestions, reduced experimentation, or fear of being replaced) through training, psychological safety initiatives, and clear role definition for both AI and human contribution.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings may be particularly relevant to organisational contexts with paternalistic leadership structures, which are more common in some Asian cultures; generalisability to Australian workplaces with different leadership styles requires careful consideration.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools by involving employees in customising or 'crafting' AI systems to fit their specific workflows — this increases collaboration and reduces resistance to AI adoption.

Paternalistic leaders can leverage their existing relationship dynamic to encourage AI crafting practices, positioning themselves as mentors who help employees shape AI tools to their needs rather than simply imposing them.
Create structured opportunities for employees to adapt and personalise AI tools to their roles, as this sense of ownership directly strengthens engagement with AI-assisted work.

articles.title: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited detail available from title and snippet alone; generalisability depends on sample size, sector diversity, and geographic scope, which are not indicated. Findings may be specific to particular industry contexts or regions.
takeaways: AI-driven workforce transformation creates a dual pathway: building employee capability and empowerment can mitigate anxiety and job insecurity — design upskilling programmes that pair technical AI training with clear career progression pathways.

Address psychological safety proactively during AI implementation by acknowledging job insecurity concerns and demonstrating how AI augments rather than replaces roles; employees who feel empowered and capable will experience lower anxiety about technological change.

Integrate sustainability and AI transformation messaging: frame AI as enabling more meaningful work and career development within a broader corporate sustainability vision, rather than as a cost-cutting or job-reduction measure.

articles.title: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings from APA; may have limited applicability to Australian workplace contexts, which differ in employment law, workplace protections, and union representation. Broader themes around worker uncertainty and psychological impact may have cross-cultural relevance.
takeaways: Monitor employee psychological wellbeing during periods of organisational change or AI implementation — uncertainty itself is a documented stressor that can affect engagement and performance independent of actual job threat.
Create transparent communication plans about AI adoption timelines and impact on roles; ambiguity amplifies anxiety more than clear (even challenging) information does.
Consider proactive support structures — counselling access, team discussions, skill-development pathways — to help workers process uncertainty rather than assuming they will adapt passively.

articles.title: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — full article needed to assess sample size, geographic scope, and sector coverage. Frontiers articles typically have global reach but generalisability depends on study design and participant demographics.
takeaways: Employee-AI collaboration may boost work engagement through dual psychological mechanisms — understanding these pathways helps identify which collaboration models (e.g. augmentation vs. automation) are most likely to sustain employee motivation and reduce disengagement.

Design AI tools and workflows with explicit attention to psychological needs (e.g. autonomy, competence, relatedness) rather than purely task efficiency — this dual focus on human psychology and AI capability is more likely to unlock sustained engagement gains.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full article — appears to be single-study research; findings may be limited by sample characteristics, industry context, and geographic scope not evident from title.
takeaways: AI adoption can negatively impact employee mental health; psychological safety and ethical leadership are critical protective factors — organisations should assess wellbeing risks before and during AI implementation.

Leaders who model ethical AI practices and create psychologically safe environments where employees can voice concerns about AI tools are better positioned to mitigate depression and disengagement during digital transformation.
When rolling out AI tools, conduct pre-deployment wellbeing assessments and establish feedback channels so employees can raise concerns without fear of retaliation.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on Deloitte's consulting experience across multiple organisations and sectors, but specific sample sizes, geographies, and sectors are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Shift your change strategy from 'AI adoption' (tool implementation) to 'AI adaptation' (building sustained human behaviours) — this reframing helps identify which specific workplace behaviours and mindsets need to change for AI tools to be used effectively.

Design targeted interventions that address behavioural barriers to AI use, rather than assuming technical training alone will drive adoption — consider what daily habits, decision-making patterns, and team norms need to shift in your organisation.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG insights are typically based on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific client details and sample composition are not disclosed. Findings may reflect biases toward large organisations that engage consulting firms.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability development challenge, not just a technology implementation — prioritise identifying which roles need which AI skills and design targeted upskilling interventions accordingly.

Embed behaviour change early in AI rollout by involving frontline employees in piloting and co-designing workflows; resistance often stems from unclear value propositions or lack of input, both addressable through structured engagement.

Create clear career pathways and role redefinition strategies during AI transition to reduce anxiety and turnover — employees need visibility on how their roles will evolve, not just assurance that jobs won't disappear.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey insights are based on their client work and industry observations, but specific organisational contexts and implementation details may vary. Findings are most applicable to large enterprises with resources for structured change programs.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling not as a technical training initiative but as a fundamental organisational change effort—this shifts mindset from 'adding a skill' to 'transforming how work gets done' and increases leadership buy-in and employee engagement.

Design change management alongside capability building: identify which roles, workflows, and decision-making processes will shift, communicate the 'why' before the 'how', and address anxiety by clarifying which human skills become more valuable as AI capabilities expand.

Structure upskilling as iterative and role-specific rather than one-size-fits-all; tailor content and pace to different employee segments (e.g., managers need different preparation than individual contributors) and build feedback loops to adjust the program as adoption unfolds.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified geographic focus or empirical data. Likely reflects US business school viewpoint and may not account for different labour markets, regulations, or organisational contexts in Australia.
takeaways: Identify specific AI-driven work changes relevant to your organisation (role redesign, skill shifts, team restructuring) and map which roles and employees will be most affected to target behaviour change interventions accordingly.

Use this as a framing tool to initiate conversations with leadership and teams about AI adoption — understanding the broad narrative helps position change management and upskilling efforts as strategic responses rather than reactive scrambles.

Consider what 'reshaping' means in your specific context: clarify whether AI will augment existing roles, create new roles, or eliminate functions, as this determines the type of behaviour change support (retraining, mindset shift, process redesign) your employees will need.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet alone. The findings suggest AI adoption can negatively impact mental health through psychological safety mechanisms, but limitations may apply based on sector, organisation type, and geographic scope.
takeaways: When introducing AI systems, actively cultivate psychological safety — create safe channels for employees to voice concerns about AI's impact without fear of repercussion, as low psychological safety appears to mediate the link between AI adoption and depression.

Leaders must model ethical AI practices explicitly; ethical leadership appears to buffer the negative mental health effects of AI adoption, so clearly communicating your organisation's AI ethics stance and decision-making rationale can reduce employee anxiety and distress.

Screen for and monitor employee wellbeing during AI rollouts — depression and mental health impacts may emerge through reduced psychological safety rather than technical challenges alone, so include wellbeing check-ins and mental health support in your change management plan.

articles.title: Agentic AI, explained - MIT Sloan
articles.snippet: Agentic AI, explained  MIT Sloan
articles.generalisability: Limited — MIT Sloan perspective on emerging technology concepts. No empirical data presented; reflects current industry thinking rather than research findings. Applicability depends on how agentic AI develops in practice.
takeaways: Understand the distinction between task-specific AI and agentic AI (systems that set goals and take autonomous action) to assess which tools are suitable for your team's workflows and decision-making boundaries.

Identify where agentic AI could reduce cognitive load in your workplace by automating multi-step processes, but establish clear governance frameworks and human oversight mechanisms before implementation to maintain control and accountability.

Use this conceptual foundation to prepare your team for conversations about AI autonomy — recognising agentic systems require different change management and training approaches than traditional automation tools.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: High — draws on established psychological research on friendship and health outcomes across diverse populations, though specific studies cited may vary in geographic scope.
takeaways: Strong friendships have measurable physiological effects: people with close friendships show lower blood pressure, reduced inflammation, and better immune function — friendship is literally good medicine, not just nice to have.

Social isolation carries health risks comparable to smoking or obesity; loneliness activates stress pathways that age the body faster — the absence of friendship is as dangerous as many recognised health hazards.

Quality beats quantity: a few genuinely close relationships protect health far more than a large social network, making intentional friendship investment more important than chasing a big friend count.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — cross-cultural research spanning multiple countries suggests music-personality links are universal rather than culturally bound.
takeaways: Your taste in music reveals something genuine about your personality that transcends geography — people from wildly different cultures show similar personality traits based on what they listen to.

This suggests music preference might be one of the few truly universal signals of personality, making it oddly reliable as a predictor across cultures in ways that language, dress, or other cultural markers are not.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Moderate — synthesises psychological research on true crime appeal, but geographic scope and specific populations studied in underlying research not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: People are drawn to true crime not out of morbid curiosity alone — psychological frameworks suggest it offers a sense of control, pattern-finding satisfaction, and safe exploration of danger from a distance.

True crime consumption reveals something counterintuitive about human psychology: we're fascinated by the very threats we evolved to fear, but consuming stories about them feels like mastery rather than vulnerability.

The appeal cuts across demographics in ways that challenge stereotypes — understanding why people binge true crime documentaries opens a window into how our brains process risk, justice, and mortality.

articles.title: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline references a study or finding but snippet provides insufficient detail to assess sample size, methodology, or geographic scope.
takeaways: The headline challenges the traditional nature-vs-nurture balance by suggesting genetics plays a larger role in personality than previously thought — counterintuitive for those who assumed upbringing and environment were dominant factors.

If personality traits are more heritable than believed, it raises intriguing questions about how much we can really 'change' ourselves through effort, and whether some workplace personality conflicts might reflect deeper biological differences rather than fixable behavioural choices.

This finding is interesting because it could reframe conversations about diversity and workplace dynamics — rather than viewing personality differences as flaws to overcome, they might be understood as natural variation rooted in biology.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reviews existing research on MBTI's predictive validity, but findings depend on quality and diversity of underlying studies; MBTI's limitations are well-documented across multiple populations.
takeaways: MBTI is widely beloved in corporate training but surprisingly weak at actually predicting who will be an effective leader — the personality types it measures don't reliably map onto leadership outcomes.

The test's four-letter categories oversimplify human personality variation; people within the same type show wildly different leadership styles and effectiveness, undermining its utility as a selection or development tool.

Despite decades of skepticism from industrial-organisational psychologists, MBTI persists in workplaces because it feels intuitive and flattering to users — not because the science supports it for leadership prediction.

articles.title: How dogs think - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: How dogs think  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Scope unclear from snippet alone; likely draws on research across multiple dog cognition studies, but breadth of evidence base cannot be assessed from title and snippet provided.
takeaways: Dogs likely process the world through scent and social cues in ways radically different from humans — they're not just furry people with four legs.
Understanding canine cognition reveals surprising parallels (and differences) in how mammals learn, remember, and bond — it's a window into the diversity of mind itself.
The 'how dogs think' question has spawned decades of fascinating research that challenges our assumptions about intelligence, emotion, and what consciousness might look like outside our species.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability limited by lack of geographic and sample details in snippet; findings on AI adoption's mental health effects warrant validation across different organisational contexts and countries, including Australian workplaces.
takeaways: Monitor employee mental health during AI implementation — depression risk increases when psychological safety is low; assess team wellbeing proactively during and after AI rollouts.

Ethical leadership is protective: leaders who model transparent AI decision-making and invite employee input on AI policies can mitigate negative psychological effects and preserve psychological safety.

Create clear psychological safety mechanisms (e.g., safe channels to voice AI concerns, no-blame feedback loops) before and during AI adoption to buffer against anxiety and depression linked to job uncertainty.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG insights are typically based on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample composition and methodology are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Create explicit norms that invite contribution from all team members regardless of hierarchy or background — psychological safety works by removing barriers to speaking up, which levels access to influence and decision-making.
Measure and track psychological safety as a workplace metric alongside performance indicators, as it directly impacts equity outcomes and engagement across diverse employee groups.

articles.title: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024 - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused survey data — findings reflect American workplace conditions, employment law, and labour practices that may not directly transfer to Australian organisations, though core psychological safety principles are universally relevant.
takeaways: Assess your team's current psychological safety baseline using validated measures (e.g., Edmondson's scale) to identify specific gaps before implementing interventions — vague perceptions of safety are hard to shift without concrete data.

Link psychological safety outcomes to measurable business metrics (retention, innovation, error reporting) when pitching safety initiatives to leadership, as this report likely demonstrates connections that justify investment in the Australian context.

Audit your feedback and speaking-up processes to ensure they actively reward candid input and learning from mistakes, not just tolerate it — passive safety (absence of threat) is weaker than active safety (invitation to contribute).

articles.title: How AI anxiety and contextual factors shape employee deviant innovation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How AI anxiety and contextual factors shape employee deviant innovation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title and snippet alone. The focus on AI anxiety and contextual factors suggests findings may apply across sectors where AI adoption creates uncertainty, though geographic scope and sample diversity are unclear.
takeaways: AI anxiety can trigger defensive or rule-breaking behaviours in employees — create psychological safety by clarifying AI's role, addressing fears directly, and involving staff in implementation planning to redirect anxiety toward constructive innovation.

Contextual factors (team norms, leadership support, clarity of expectations) mediate how anxiety translates into behaviour — design interventions around these levers rather than assuming anxiety alone drives outcomes.

articles.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey research typically draws on global client work and surveys, but findings reflect practices in large organisations and may not generalise to small-to-medium enterprises or non-Western contexts.
takeaways: Create psychological safety by framing AI as a tool that augments human capabilities rather than replaces them, allowing employees to experiment with AI tools without fear of failure or job loss.

Design clear governance structures and transparent guidelines for AI use that empower employees to make decisions autonomously while maintaining oversight—this balance reduces anxiety and increases engagement with new technologies.
Invest in upskilling programmes that help employees understand AI's strengths and limitations, enabling them to use tools confidently and speak up about risks or concerns without feeling inadequate.

articles.title: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety - Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.source: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.snippet: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety  Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents conceptual clarifications from a Harvard institution but lacks empirical data or specific sample; applicability depends on which misconceptions are addressed and whether examples are geographically bound.
takeaways: Clarify what psychological safety actually is (likely addressing common myths like 'anything goes' culture or absence of accountability) so you can communicate the concept accurately when building it in your team.
Use debunked misconceptions as a diagnostic tool — identify which false beliefs about psychological safety exist in your organisation and address them directly in training or change conversations.
